newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan unveils tough new press law.
newsitem.headline: Jordan unveils tough new press law.

text.p: King Hussein has unveiled tough revisions to Jordan's press law, tightening restrictions on reporting and stiffening fines for offenders, just days after lashing out at the "deteriorating morals" of journalists.

A royal decree issued late on Saturday follows criticism by King Hussein of Jordan's "yellow press" -- the numerous weekly opposition papers which authorities accuse of being mouthpieces for foreigners undermining national stability.

The decree for the first time prevents non-Jordanians from editing newspapers and sharply raises financial hurdles facing newspaper owners. It also cancels a pledge to sell the state's controlling stake in Jordan's top-selling newspaper, Al-Rai.

The government has "ensured that the journalistic freedom will be a responsible freedom at the service of the country and its people," Information Minister Samir Mutawae told the state Petra news agency.
The revised law forbids journalists outright from writing about Jordan's armed forces and security services.

It expands the "10 Commandments", a central article in the law listing 10 areas off limits to journalists, to include an 11th catch-all ban on subjects..."which include false information or rumours which lead to harming the general interest, or government institutions, or its workers".

It retains existing bans on anything which offends the king and royal family, contains contempt of religion, damages national unity, encourages crime, undermines confidence in the Jordanian dinar or offends public morals.

The prohibitions cover drawings and pictures as well as written articles. Fines for violators were raised to at least 15,000 dinars ($21,200) from 1,000 dinars. Offending newspapers can be suspended from publication.
"The press is not reflecting the correct image about the country which we know," King Hussein told senior army officers in a speech last week. "This distortion should stop."

He said Jordan's press was suffering from "deteriorating morals", citing criticism of democracy in Jordan and what he said were untrue stories that he donated $300,000 to families of Israeli schoolgirls shot dead by a Jordanian soldier.
The revised law also cancels a government commitment to cut its stake in the leading dailies Al-Rai and Ad-Dustour to 30 percent from 61 percent and 32 percent respectively.

Weekly papers, many of whom have a circulation of just a few thousand, have been given just three months to increase their capital to 300,000 dinars from 15,000 dinars. Journalists said the new financial requirements would force many to close.

Unlike the staid pro-government dailies, Jordan's weeklies, which number at least 30, are often boisterous opposition papers, splashing their front pages with stories of political corruption and popular discontent at Jordan's peace treaty with Israel.

A number of weekly journalists have already been tried this year for ruffling conservative sensibilities in Jordan. Some of them, tried under penal law instead of the press law, received prison terms of up to nine months.
